name: AdaptedMind
line: AdaptedMind makes elementary math practice a game; AMP runs to precalculus on published mastery and review rules.
description: AMP vs AdaptedMind: what each costs, what AdaptedMind has shown, and how AMP's published mastery and review rules carry a learner through precalculus.
verdict: AdaptedMind is a low-priced math program for the elementary grades, with points, badges and a teacher's video for every missed problem, and Trustpilot reviewers rate it 4.5 of 5 [1][4][7]. It says an algorithm adjusts difficulty to each student [1]. AMP publishes its rules for when a skill counts as learned and when it comes back, keeps a level in each of 14 strands, and runs from counting through precalculus.

reasons.title: AMP says exactly what counts as learned
reasons.body: AdaptedMind's home page says an algorithm finds each student's strengths and weaknesses and adjusts the difficulty [1]. On the AdaptedMind pages we read, we found no rule for when a skill counts as learned [1]. In AMP a skill is Strong when four of the last five answers are right without help. An answer given after a hint or the lesson is recorded, but it does not count.

reasons.title: Old skills come back on a fixed schedule
reasons.body: AdaptedMind's home page mentions automatic assessments on new and old skills, with no schedule given [1]. AMP brings each learned skill back after 6 hours, 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks and a month, mixed with other topics, and a miss starts the schedule over. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [10].

reasons.title: A level in each part of math, adjusted every answer
reasons.body: AdaptedMind sets its starting point with a pretest, then adjusts difficulty as a student practices [1]. Reviews quoted by Brighterly, a company that sells its own tutoring, report work beyond a child's abilities or at the wrong grade level [5]. AMP has no separate test. It keeps a level in each of 14 strands of math, places the learner within the first 24 problems, and chooses every next problem from the answers: new work, a prerequisite, or review.

reasons.title: Help before the answer, worked steps after every one
reasons.body: When a child misses a problem, one of AdaptedMind's teachers explains it in a video [1]. AMP offers a one-step hint and a written lesson with a worked example before the learner answers. The hint never gives the answer away. After every answer, right or wrong, AMP shows the correct answer and the worked steps.

reasons.title: It runs through high school math
reasons.body: AdaptedMind's home page calls it a K-6 curriculum [1]. Its grade picker goes to grade 8, where grades 6, 7 and 8 each list 172 lessons and "more coming soon" [12]. AMP runs from counting through Algebra 1, Geometry, Algebra 2 and Precalculus: 336 skills on one prerequisite map. A learner ready for algebra at ten, or still building fractions at fourteen, stays in the same program.

rows.price: $9.95 per month, recurring monthly, after a 30-day free trial. Includes up to 5 children, per its sign-up page [4].
rows.buyers: Families and teachers. Teachers at public or nonprofit schools get a 30-day free trial for up to 35 students [3].
rows.range: Its home page calls it a K-6 curriculum [1]. Its grade picker lists grades 1 to 8; grades 6 to 8 are labeled as still growing [12].
rows.start: A pretest sets the starting point in the curriculum [1].
rows.teaching: When a problem is missed, one of its teachers explains it in a video. AdaptedMind says it has over 10,000 explanation videos [1].
rows.next: An algorithm finds strengths and weaknesses and adjusts difficulty [1]. We found no published rules for how.
rows.mastery: We found no mastery rule on the AdaptedMind pages we read [1].
rows.review: Formative assessments on new and old skills, per its home page [1]. We found no review schedule.
rows.adult: Little, by its account: a child works independently, and reports can go straight to a parent's inbox [1].
rows.reports: Real-time data and reports by email. Classroom reporting for teachers [1].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found. No entry in Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report, as of November 2026 [8][9].

theirs: AdaptedMind is an online math program its home page calls a K-6 curriculum [1]. It comes from GloWorld, LLC, a United States company founded in 2010, according to EdTech Impact [3]. AdaptedMind says more than 2 million parents in nearly 200 countries have chosen it [1]. It sells to families and teachers, and it also sells reading, science and social studies [2][3][5].

Each student starts with a pretest that sets the starting point [1]. Practice is dressed as a game, with points, badges, monsters and characters [1][5]. When a problem is missed, one of AdaptedMind's teachers explains it in a video [1]. Reports can be sent to a parent's email [1]. AdaptedMind says it holds over 300,000 math problems and explanations and over 10,000 explanation videos [1].
credit: A game layer with points, badges and monsters, which many reviewers say children enjoy [1][5][7]. AMP has no games, avatars or badges.
A low price: $9.95 a month after a 30-day free trial, covering up to five children [4]. AMP costs more.
A large library of teacher-made explanation videos, over 10,000 by its own count [1]. AMP has far fewer films.
An app as well as the website [6], and reading, science and social studies from the same company [2][5]. AMP has no app in the stores and teaches only math.
Trustpilot reviewers rate it 4.5 of 5 across 1,125 reviews [7].

theirs: We found no outcome study of AdaptedMind on its home page, in Evidence for ESSA or in the What Works Clearinghouse's intervention reports, as of November 2026 [1][8][9]. That means no randomized trial, no matched comparison and no company-run study that we could find.

Its home page calls the curriculum "research-based, common core aligned, and comprehensive" and cites no study [1]. EdTech Impact's listing calls it evidence-based, also without a study or an ESSA tier [3]. The numbers AdaptedMind puts forward are about reach: more than 2 million parents and over 400 million problems solved [1]. Reach is not a learning result.
ours: AMP's review and teaching rules come from well-tested findings. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed, spaced practice scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks on the researchers' own test [10]. Worked examples improve math performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 across 55 studies [11]. AdaptedMind explains a missed problem in a video [1]. AMP gives every problem type a lesson with a worked example, shows worked steps after every answer, and adds a published rule for when a skill is learned and a fixed schedule for when it comes back. We expect that to show in outcomes, and we have committed in public to measuring it.

AMP is new, and its own outcome studies have not run yet. They begin in 2027: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. Until then, the research behind each part of AMP is laid out in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child is in the elementary grades and practices longer for points, badges and characters.
You want a low monthly price, with one membership for up to five children.
You want an app on a phone or tablet.
You want reading, science and social studies from the same company.
amp: You want to know exactly what counts as learned: four of the last five right without help.
You want old skills to come back on a schedule, without planning it.
Your learner is past grade 6, or soon will be. AMP runs through precalculus.
You want a hint that gives the first step, and the worked steps after every answer.
You want paper too: workbooks made for your child, each with a worked answer key.

questions.question: Is AMP more expensive than AdaptedMind?
questions.answer: Yes. AMP costs $599 a year or $59 a month for the first child, and $399 a year or $39 a month for each additional child. AdaptedMind's sign-up page gives $9.95 a month after a 30-day free trial, for up to 5 children [4]. AMP's price covers counting through precalculus, a level in each of 14 strands, scheduled review and unlimited printable workbooks, and it is free to start with 100 answers and 5 workbooks per learner.

questions.question: What grades does AdaptedMind cover?
questions.answer: Its home page calls it a K-6 curriculum [1], and its grade picker lists grades 1 to 8, with grades 6 to 8 labeled as still growing [12]. AMP runs from counting through precalculus in one program.

questions.question: Does AMP have games like AdaptedMind?
questions.answer: No. AdaptedMind rewards practice with points, badges and monsters [1]. AMP's reward is plainer: +1 XP for each right answer without help, and a record of every skill grown.

questions.question: Has AdaptedMind been shown to work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of it, and no entry in Evidence for ESSA or a What Works Clearinghouse intervention report, as of November 2026 [8][9]. Where AMP's own evidence stands is set out in the evidence section of this page.
